However, other results have largely failed to substantiate any benefit for secondary prevention. No reduction in the incidence of new skin cancers,11-13 or in malignant transformation of cervi- cal dysplasia,14 or in new colorectal adenomas15 was reported in other studies. In a primary prevention study, a combination of betacarotene, vitamin E, and selenium was associated with a re- duction in stomach and oesophageal cancers in a population at high risk of these cancers and with a diet low in micronutrients in China.16 In contrast, other primary prevention studies have failed to show any benefit, and possibly some harm, from betac- arotene supplements in well-nourished populations. A study in smokers17-19 showed an increase in lung cancer and associated mortality in those receiving betacarotene, but not those receiving vitamin E. Similarly, an increased risk of lung cancer was noted in recipients of betacarotene with vitamin A in another study in individuals at high risk of lung cancer, and this study was stopped early as a result.20,21 In a 6-year follow-up,22 this risk was found to persist, albeit at lower and not statistically significant levels. A third study in healthy men found no benefit or harm for betacar- otene supplements in terms of incidence of malignant neo- plasms, including those of the lung;23 a subgroup analysis of this study suggested that supplementation may reduce the risk of prostate cancer in those men with low baseline betacarotene lev- els.24 Among subjects with colorectal adenoma,25 who neither smoked nor drank alcohol, betacarotene supplementation was associated with a decrease in the risk of recurrent adenoma, but risk was increased in those who smoked or drank alcohol. A meta-analysis26 of trials of antoxidant supplementation found that betacarotene had no anticarcinogenic effects on gastrointes- tinal cancer, and that given alone, it increased mortality. When given with vitamin A and E, mortality increased further. A fur- ther systematic review and meta-analysis27 found that betacaro- tene supplementation was associated with an increased incidence of cancer among smokers, but not among non-smokers. There was also a trend towards increased cancer mortality with betac- arotene supplementation. Vitamin C has also been proposed for prevention of malignancy but there is no real evidence to justify it.
